strengths: Addresses an important problem: training vector-quantized networks with useful encoder and codebook gradients while reducing auxiliary-loss requirements.
The directional surrogate is simple, and the reconstruction experiments show promising improvements across five datasets, multiple codebook sizes, and residual quantization.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail and ablations on learning rate, batch size, noise variance, deterministic variants, and codebook replacement. Reconstruction results are averaged over three runs.
Applying the proposed replacement procedure to competing methods improves fairness compared with giving this advantage only to the proposed method.
weaknesses: Central claims about hard forward assignments and absence of train–test mismatch contradict the method actually evaluated. At nonzero noise variance, Eq. (8) generally does not output the selected codeword, whereas inference uses hard nearest-neighbor quantization. Experiments use variances of 0.001 and 0.01. SF-DiVeQ additionally trains with random interpolations, whose relationship to hard inference is insufficiently explained. Exact hard assignments apply to the deterministic DiVeQ variant, not the main stochastic method.

The claim of unbiased codebook gradients is unsupported and generally false for the hard-quantization objective. Writing u = (c−z)/||c−z||, the zero-noise surrogate gives codebook Jacobian uuᵀ and encoder Jacobian I−uuᵀ; within a fixed assignment region, hard quantization instead has Jacobians I and 0. The stop-gradient construction is therefore a surrogate estimator, not an unbiased consequence of reparameterization. Moreover, Eq. (10) omits the noise dependence present in Eq. (8).

Claims that SF-DiVeQ ensures full utilization and prevents misalignment lack a guarantee or sufficiently controlled evidence. Segments that are never selected need not receive gradients. SF-DiVeQ uniquely receives unquantized pretraining and specialized latent-based initialization, but these advantages are not separately ablated or supplied to baselines. Appendix A.5 explicitly makes successful utilization depend on these initialization choices.

The misalignment analysis misapplies Shannon rate–distortion theory. Monotonicity of an optimal rate–distortion frontier does not require independently trained finite neural models to improve whenever codebook size increases. Nonmonotonic reconstruction curves therefore do not establish codebook misalignment. Selected t-SNE plots and distortion divided by entropy do not resolve this causal attribution; latent distortion also depends on representation scale.

Generation results do not support the broad superiority claims. In Table 2, DiVeQ is worse than STE at 9, 10, and 12 bits. In Table 6, SF-DiVeQ is worse than STE at every tested bitrate on FFHQ and LSUN Bedroom. Improvements are selective, and uncertainty estimates are absent for FID and the three-run reconstruction averages, making small differences difficult to assess.

The evaluation does not cleanly isolate the contribution beyond existing NSVQ and SFVQ. A matched SFVQ baseline and controlled combinations of quantization geometry, gradient estimator, and initialization are missing. The claim of requiring no hyperparameter tuning or special heuristics is also overstated: noise variance changes between tasks, DiVeQ uses scheduled codebook replacement, and SF-DiVeQ requires specialized initialization. These unresolved methodological and evidential issues outweigh the promising reconstruction results.

strengths: Addresses an important problem in training vector-quantized models with a simple surrogate that propagates reconstruction gradients to both encoder and codebook without commitment or codebook losses.
Reconstruction experiments span five datasets, eight codebook sizes, and three runs, with generally favorable results against STE, EMA, rotation trick, Gumbel-Softmax, and NSVQ.
The appendix provides substantial implementation details and useful ablations on noise variance, learning rate, batch size, deterministic variants, and residual quantization.
weaknesses: The claim of unbiased codebook gradients is incorrect for hard VQ. Writing u = (c − z)/||c − z||, the zero-noise surrogate gives codebook Jacobian uuᵀ and encoder Jacobian I − uuᵀ, whereas hard nearest-neighbor quantization has local Jacobians I and zero within an assignment region. These are surrogate gradients, not an unbiased reparameterization of hard VQ. Equation (10) also omits the noise used in Equation (8).

Hard forward assignments and absence of train–test mismatch are contradicted by the actual method. With nonzero noise, Equation (8) generally does not output a codeword; experiments use variances of 10⁻³ and 10⁻². SF-DiVeQ trains with interpolated points between codewords, while evaluation uses hard nearest-codeword assignments. Its interpolation mismatch remains even at zero noise.

Claims of guaranteed full utilization, prevention of misalignment, and freedom from special heuristics are unsupported. Unselected segments can still receive no gradients. SF-DiVeQ additionally uses a unique warm-up and carefully prescribed latent-based initialization, without a matched initialization ablation separating these effects from the proposed update rule.

The misalignment analysis misapplies Shannon rate–distortion theory: monotonicity of the optimal distortion–rate function does not require separately trained finite neural models to improve monotonically with codebook size, especially across different perceptual metrics. Selected t-SNE examples and distortion divided by entropy do not establish the claimed causal explanation.

Generation results do not support broad superiority. In Table 6, both proposed methods lose to STE at every AFHQ codebook size; at 12 bits on FFHQ, DiVeQ and SF-DiVeQ obtain FIDs of 8.22 and 8.60 versus 4.73 for the rotation trick. Reconstruction results report averages without uncertainty, and generation results lack reported variability, weakening conclusions about small gains.

Novelty and experimental isolation remain incomplete. DiVeQ modifies NSVQ's noise direction, and SF-DiVeQ incorporates an existing SFVQ construction, but there is no controlled comparison isolating the new gradient rule from the inherited interpolation mechanism. Relevant structured quantizers such as FSQ, LFQ, and BSQ are discussed but not evaluated.

strengths: Addresses an important problem in training discrete latent representations with a simple directional surrogate that propagates reconstruction gradients to both encoder and codebook without separate commitment or codebook losses.
Reconstruction experiments show consistent improvements across five image datasets, multiple codebook sizes, and three metrics. Residual-VQ experiments provide additional evidence of applicability.

The appendix includes substantial implementation detail and useful ablations on batch size, learning rate, noise variance, deterministic variants, and codebook replacement. Reconstruction results are averaged over three runs.
weaknesses: The claimed unbiased codebook gradients are not justified. In the zero-noise limit, writing u = (c − z)/||c − z||, the stop-gradient construction gives surrogate Jacobians J_z = I − uuᵀ and J_c = uuᵀ. For hard nearest-neighbor quantization with a locally fixed assignment, the actual Jacobians are J_z = 0 and J_c = I. The method is therefore a biased surrogate, not an unbiased reparameterization gradient. Equation (10) also omits the noise used in the actual method.

Central claims about hard forward assignments and absence of train–test mismatch contradict the implemented method. With the nonzero variances used experimentally, Equation (8) generally does not output a codeword. SF-DiVeQ trains on random interpolations between codewords, whereas evaluation uses hard nearest-codeword assignment. These discrepancies need explicit analysis rather than being marked absent in Table 1.

The claims of requiring no hyperparameter tuning or special heuristics are overstated. Different noise variances are selected for compression and generation, and Appendix C.5 explicitly treats variance as a generalization hyperparameter. DiVeQ uses scheduled codebook replacement, while SF-DiVeQ requires a special warm-up and initialization procedure. Matched initialization ablations are needed to isolate the benefit of SF-DiVeQ.

The explanation of codebook misalignment misuses rate–distortion theory. An optimal rate–distortion envelope does not require independently trained finite neural models to improve monotonically with codebook size. Consequently, nonmonotonic reconstruction curves and selected t-SNE plots do not establish misalignment as the cause. The guarantee of full utilization is also unsupported: adjacent codewords can remain unupdated when neither incident segment is selected.

Generation results do not support broad superiority claims. In Table 6, neither proposed method beats the best baseline at any AFHQ bitrate. On FFHQ at 12 bits, DiVeQ and SF-DiVeQ obtain FIDs of 8.22 and 8.60 versus 4.73 for RT. The evidence supports competitive performance in some settings, with meaningful regressions elsewhere.

Important comparisons and uncertainty estimates are missing. SFVQ is the direct precursor to SF-DiVeQ but is not evaluated to isolate the new gradient rule; FSQ and other cited alternatives addressing collapse are also absent. Reconstruction averages lack variability estimates, and generation results lack repeated-run uncertainty. These omissions make modest improvements over strong baselines difficult to assess.

strengths: Addresses an important problem in learning discrete representations. DiVeQ provides a compact surrogate that propagates reconstruction-loss gradients to both encoder and codebook without additional commitment or codebook losses.

The empirical study is broad: five image datasets, image reconstruction and generation, speech coding, and residual quantization. Image reconstruction results averaged over three runs show promising improvements over several established quantization methods.

The appendix includes substantial implementation details and useful ablations on noise variance, initialization, codebook replacement, learning rate, batch size, and deterministic variants. Applying the proposed replacement procedure to competing methods is a constructive comparison choice.
weaknesses: The central hard-assignment and no-train–test-mismatch claims contradict the implemented formulation. For nonzero noise variance, Eq. (8) generally does not output the nearest codeword, whereas inference explicitly uses hard nearest-neighbor assignment. Exact agreement occurs only in the zero-noise limit. This distinction matters because Fig. 11 shows that removing noise reduces DiVeQ's performance. SF-DiVeQ also changes from randomly sampled interpolation points during training to nearest-curve projection at inference.

The claim of unbiased codebook gradients is unsupported and inconsistent with the stop-gradient construction. Let u=(c−z)/||c−z||. In the zero-noise limit, the surrogate Jacobians are J_z=I−uu^T and J_c=uu^T, whereas hard assignment within a fixed assignment region has J_z=0 and J_c=I. Thus, these are surrogate gradients, not the exact hard-quantizer derivatives. Eq. (10) also omits the stochastic direction appearing in Eq. (8). No objective or argument establishes unbiasedness.

SF-DiVeQ's compression comparison lacks essential rate accounting. A nearest point on a continuous segment requires both a segment index and an interpolation coordinate, yet results are compared using only log2(K) codebook bits. The manuscript does not specify how that coordinate is quantized or transmitted, or measure the resulting total bitrate. Consequently, improved reconstruction could reflect additional representational capacity rather than better performance at equal rate. How continuous curve locations become discrete transformer targets and generated latents is also insufficiently explained.

Claims that SF-DiVeQ ensures full utilization and avoids misalignment are stronger than the evidence. Unselected segments and their endpoints need not receive updates, so connectivity alone does not guarantee recovery of every inactive codeword. Main experiments use special initialization, while Appendix C.7 reports degradation for large randomly initialized codebooks and investigates substantially increased codebook learning rates. These findings qualify the claims of guaranteed utilization and training without special heuristics.

The rate-distortion argument used to diagnose misalignment is incorrect. Shannon's optimal rate-distortion function does not require independently trained finite neural models to improve monotonically with codebook size. Optimization variability and differing learned representations can produce nonmonotonic results without establishing the proposed cause. Selected t-SNE visualizations and distortion divided by index entropy do not establish causality or provide a scale-invariant comparison across learned latent spaces.

The evidence does not support consistent superiority across tasks. In Table 2, DiVeQ is worse than STE at 9, 10, and 12 bits under the first configuration; Table 7 also contains substantial DiVeQ failures under the second configuration. Speech results frequently favor EMA in some settings. Reconstruction experiments average three runs but omit variability, and generation and speech tables do not establish statistical reliability. More calibrated claims and uncertainty estimates are needed.

Important comparisons remain missing: particularly SFVQ, whose interpolation construction directly underlies SF-DiVeQ, and modern alternatives such as FSQ or LFQ. The heavily modified speech codec also limits conclusions about standard DAC systems. Overall, the promising empirical observations do not resolve the foundational gradient claims or establish a fair compression comparison.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: training vector quantizers through reconstruction objectives without separate codebook and commitment losses. The proposed surrogate is simple and potentially useful.

Substantial experimental coverage includes five image datasets, speech coding, and residual VQ. Image reconstruction results averaged over three runs show promising improvements over several established estimators.
The appendix provides useful implementation details and ablations on noise variance, initialization, codebook replacement, learning rate, batch size, and deterministic variants.
weaknesses: The claimed unbiased gradients are not justified by the construction. In the zero-noise limit, writing u=(c-z)/||c-z||, the stop-gradient surrogate yields Jacobians I-uuᵀ for z and uuᵀ for the selected codeword. These differ from the hard quantizer's local Jacobians, 0 and I, away from assignment boundaries. This is a custom biased gradient estimator, not an established unbiased reparameterization gradient. Equation (10) also omits the noise used in Equation (8).

Hard forward assignments and absence of train–test mismatch are incorrectly claimed for the main method. With the nonzero variances actually used, Equation (8) generally does not output the selected codeword, whereas inference uses hard nearest-neighbor assignment. SF-DiVeQ likewise trains with random interpolations but tests using the nearest curve point. Small noise does not establish exact equivalence.

SF-DiVeQ's compression comparisons lack adequate rate accounting. A continuous curve point requires both a segment index and an interpolation coordinate, but results are compared using codebook bits alone. The manuscript does not specify the coordinate's quantization, transmission cost, or treatment by the autoregressive generator. Consequently, equal-rate reconstruction gains and compatibility with discrete-token generation remain unestablished.

The misalignment analysis misapplies Shannon's rate-distortion theory. Optimal rate-distortion behavior does not guarantee monotonically improving metrics for separately trained, finite neural models. Nonmonotonic results therefore do not establish codebook misalignment, and selected t-SNE plots do not prove it causes the failures. The distortion-per-bit comparison also lacks control for differing latent scales.

Claims of guaranteed full utilization and freedom from special heuristics exceed the evidence. Unselected segments can leave their endpoints without gradients. SF-DiVeQ uses a special warm start and initialization; Appendix C.7 shows degradation with random initialization for large codebooks and explores codebook learning-rate multipliers of 10–50 to recover performance.

The evaluation does not establish consistent superiority. In Table 2, DiVeQ loses to STE at 9, 10, and 12 bits under the first training setting; Table 7 also contains substantial DiVeQ failures. Reconstruction averages lack uncertainty estimates, and generation and speech results lack reported run-to-run uncertainty. Fixed auxiliary-loss coefficients and unequal initialization further limit conclusions about comparative robustness.

Important comparisons and practical validation are missing: a direct SFVQ baseline would isolate the benefit beyond the existing curve construction, and FSQ/LFQ would test the utilization motivation against relevant alternatives. Speech experiments substantially simplify DAC and remove its low-dimensional quantization bottleneck, limiting transfer of the conclusions to established codecs.

strengths: The proposed quantization surrogate is simple and practically motivated: it supplies encoder and codebook updates from the task loss without separate commitment or codebook losses.

The empirical study is broad, covering five image datasets, image reconstruction and generation, speech coding, and residual quantization. Image reconstruction results show encouraging improvements across codebook sizes.

The appendix provides substantial implementation details and useful ablations on noise variance, initialization, replacement, learning rate, and batch size. Reporting image reconstruction averages over three runs and applying replacement to competing methods are positive experimental choices.
weaknesses: The claim of unbiased codebook gradients is not supported and conflicts with the stopped-gradient construction. In the zero-noise limit, writing u = (c−z)/||c−z||, the surrogate codebook Jacobian is uuᵀ, whereas the hard assignment has Jacobian I with respect to the selected codeword within a fixed assignment region. The encoder Jacobian is likewise a surrogate, I−uuᵀ, rather than the true zero Jacobian. This can be a useful estimator, but invoking reparameterization does not establish unbiasedness.

SF-DiVeQ's compression comparisons lack essential rate accounting. Section 4 evaluates projection onto the nearest point of a continuous curve, which requires both a segment index and an interpolation coordinate to reconstruct. The paper reports only codebook bits, without specifying how that coordinate is quantized or transmitted. Consequently, equal codebook size does not establish equal bitrate. How the discrete VQGAN transformer represents or generates the interpolation coordinate is also insufficiently explained.

The claims of exact hard forward assignments and no train–test mismatch do not hold for the reported finite-noise implementation: Eq. (8) generally produces a point different from the selected codeword, while inference uses hard nearest-neighbor assignment. SF-DiVeQ additionally changes from randomly sampled interpolation points during training to nearest-curve projection at inference. These distinctions should be acknowledged and measured.

Claims that SF-DiVeQ guarantees full utilization and avoids misalignment are stronger than the evidence. Unselected segments need not receive gradients, and Appendix C.7 documents initialization-dependent utilization and performance. Moreover, nonmonotonic reconstruction quality across separately trained codebook sizes does not violate Shannon rate-distortion theory or establish misalignment; t-SNE plots do not establish the claimed causal explanation.

The performance claims overstate the results. In Table 2 under HP1, DiVeQ trails STE at 9, 10, and 12 bits; in Table 3, EMA exceeds DiVeQ on several speech metrics. Missing uncertainty estimates make small differences difficult to assess. Baseline-specific tuning is limited, and the heavily modified single-codebook speech model restricts conclusions about standard DAC.

The SF extension builds directly on existing SFVQ, but lacks a controlled comparison using the same curve quantizer with alternative gradient estimators. Such an experiment is needed to separate benefits of additional representational capacity from the proposed training rule. Together with the gradient and bitrate issues, this prevents the otherwise promising empirical results from supporting acceptance.
